RagShortTexts: Hulagu's sack of Baghdad in 1258 extinguished the Abbasid Caliphate, ending the Islamic.

Variants.Content: In February 1258 Hulagu Khan's army broke into Baghdad after a siege, and the sack that followed killed people in the hundreds of thousands by most estimates. Caliph al-Musta'sim was trampled to death, ending the Abbasid line that had ruled from the city since 762. The House of Wisdom, the great library of the age, was ransacked and its manuscripts thrown into the Tigris. The canal networks that fed the region's fields were damaged, and irrigation that once supported dense farming began to decline. Chroniclers later described the river running black with ink and red with blood. The disaster removed the caliph who had been the symbolic head of Sunni Islam, leaving the Mamluks and the Ilkhanate to fight over the Near East without a spiritual centre in Baghdad.
Five centuries of Islamic scholarship drowned in days. Surviving scholars carried scorched folios to Cairo, weeping at the extinction of classical Arabic and Persian learning.

The fall of Baghdad split the Islamic world into rival centres, so caliphal legitimacy had to be rebuilt elsewhere. The Mamluk sultans in Cairo later installed an Abbasid survivor as a titular caliph and used the restored line to justify their war against the Mongols. A lord in Syria or Egypt who wanted a patent of rule had to weigh that legitimacy against the Ilkhanate's growing power.
